prompt: Put the thirty-second reader's three questions in order.
hint: Most weeks the reader stops after the first.

prompt: Which phrase is part of Stephen Few's definition of a dashboard?

choices.why: The opposite: the most important information only.
On a single screen, at a glance, not after study.

choices.text: Updated every second so that the reader always sees the latest value
choices.why: Refresh rate is not in the definition.
Not in the definition the lesson quotes.

prompt: On Faro's old dashboard, where was the first-delivery on-time rate?
hint: Easy data, not the right questions.

choices.text: In a gauge in the second row
choices.why: That was the overall rate, 94.5%, coloured green.
The map showed orders.

choices.text: Behind a click on the delivery tile, two levels down in the drill-down
choices.why: It was not on the dashboard in any form.
The one number that mattered most was missing entirely.

prompt: Which part of a dashboard is the most valuable space, for a left-to-right reader?

choices.text: The centre, because a screen draws the eye to its middle before anything else
choices.why: The habit the lesson designs for is top left.
It belongs to the answer to "are we all right?".
The last place the eye reaches.
Filters are zoom, not overview.

prompt: Shneiderman's phrase: overview first, zoom and filter, then details on ___.
How many tiles did Faro's old operations dashboard have?
Where does the table of the ten largest customers belong?

choices.why: That space is for whether things are fine.
Zone 3 is the trend.
It is a detail, and details come on demand.
Nothing about customers is compared with that target.

prompt: "84.1%" alone on a tile. What does the lesson say it lacks?

choices.why: A target, the previous period, a trend.
It already has one.
Size does not say whether it is good.
Decoration.

prompt: Match each comparison to the question it answers.
hint: Three comparisons a tile can carry.

prompt: Why is Faro's target for first deliveries 95%?
hint: Treat a new customer like an old one.

choices.why: The lesson gives a reason beyond that.
The contract promises two working days, not a rate.

choices.text: It is what renewals already reach
choices.why: Renewals arrive on time 95.1% of the time.

choices.text: The board set it at its quarterly meeting after seeing Marina's presentation
choices.why: Not where the number comes from.

prompt: The weekly first-delivery rate stayed between 80.4% and 85.0% for six months. What message does the sparkline carry?

choices.text: A sudden drop that needs an emergency response from the warehouse this week
choices.why: There was no drop; the level has been steady all year.

choices.text: It has been about this bad all year
choices.why: A chronic problem, which calls for a different response from a sudden one.
No trend upwards.
Its shape is the message.

prompt: What should decide a tile's colour?
hint: The old gauge was green at 94.5%.

choices.text: A fixed threshold, such as green above 90%
choices.why: A judgement written once and forgotten.

choices.text: The comparison the reader actually cares about
choices.why: Below target is one colour; at or above is neutral.
Brand is not meaning.
A big number is not a good one.

prompt: Why is the 90-day cancellation rate a lagging indicator?

choices.why: Who reports it is not the point.
Frequency is not lag.
It is the outcome Faro cares about most.

choices.text: It is only known ninety days later
choices.why: Today's dashboard shows customers who joined three months ago.

prompt: When is a leading indicator worth watching?

choices.text: When it is easy to collect
choices.why: Easy data is how the old dashboard went wrong.

choices.text: When it really does move before the outcome
choices.why: Late first boxes go with more than double the cancellations, so the rate leads.
Frequency without a link to the outcome is noise.

choices.text: When the board has asked for it in writing after seeing it in another company's dashboard
choices.why: A request does not make it predictive.

prompt: Why keep the lagging measure on the dashboard as well?

choices.text: To check the two still move together
choices.why: When they stop, that is itself a finding.

choices.text: Because dashboards need at least two tiles
choices.why: No such rule.

choices.text: For symmetry with the tile next to it
choices.why: Layout is not the reason.
Not the reason given.

prompt: Which of these are leading indicators for Faro's cancellations? Choose all that apply.
hint: Seen now, moves before the outcome.

choices.text: Share of first boxes on time this week
choices.why: Established by the analysis.

choices.text: Ninety-day cancellation rate of the June cohort
choices.why: That is the outcome itself, measured late.
A lagging financial result.
Nothing links it to early cancellations.

prompt: What did Stephen Few design to replace the gauge?
hint: A bar, a target line, bands.

choices.why: That was Tufte, for trends.
More than a gauge in a fraction of the space.
Not from this lesson.
Not a gauge replacement.

prompt: Faro's map coloured by orders showed what, by the lesson?
hint: Where do most orders come from in any business?

choices.why: It was coloured by orders, not delays.
A map earns its space only when location is the question.

choices.text: Which customers are most profitable for Faro across the state of São Paulo
choices.why: Orders are not profit.
Not what it was coloured by.

prompt: Somebody asks for a presentation of the finding and is sent a link to the dashboard. What does the lesson say is wrong?

choices.text: Dashboards are slower to load than slides
choices.why: Not the argument.

choices.text: The dashboard might be out of date
choices.why: It might, and that is not the main problem.

choices.text: Links get lost in email threads that have more than a few replies
choices.why: Not the lesson's point.

choices.text: It leaves the analysis to the reader
choices.why: Marina's first meeting in a more expensive format. Use the dashboard to notice, and the story to decide.

prompt: Put each label on the dashboard problem it names.
hint: Read it as the thirty-second reader.

labels.text: a gauge where a bar would do
a pie cut into too many slices
a number with nothing to compare it to
the key number where the eye arrives last
a map when location is not the question
